section_summary: This section contains United States diplomatic despatches, intelligence reports, and press translations from 1942 to 1944 examining internal wartime conditions and political dynamics in Japan. Key records document deteriorating civilian health, severe food rationing, labor unrest, and air raid anxieties in Japan; the reorganization of the Diet under the totalitarian Imperial Rule Assistance Political Society; the fall of the Tojo Cabinet and formation of the Koiso government in July 1944; Japanese economic propaganda maneuvering in the occupied Philippines; and intelligence on the postwar platform of the Japanese Communist Party gathered by American observers in Yenan.

subfiles.about: Transmits a report from Sian based on an interview with a Chinese medical student detailing health deterioration, food rationing, and severe labor conditions in Japan.
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Ambassador, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Gauss forwards Sian report from a Chinese student who left Tokyo in September 1943: shortages of doctors and medicines, rising tuberculosis, tight rationing, 12-hour shifts and air-raid anxiety.
subfiles.title: Chungking Despatch No. 2301: Report on Conditions in Japan Indicating Deterioration in Health of Japanese

subfiles.about: Transmits a Foreign Economic Administration intelligence report based on an interview with a Chinese woman who traveled extensively in Japan in October 1943.
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Ambassador, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss forwards a confidential Foreign Economic Administration report summarizing an interview with a young Chinese woman who visited Japan in October 1943 before traveling to Chungking. She detailed travel by convoy and rail across Moji, Kobe, Yokohama, and Tokyo, noting charcoal-burning taxis, strict nighttime blackouts throughout Japan and Korea, and numerous air-raid ditches dug across Tokyo. The report highlights severe food rationing and tiny meal portions, the thriving Tokyo black market, foreigners relying on German acquaintances to make store purchases, and Japanese security demands that travelers conceal Japan's inferior food situation compared to occupied Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Chungking Despatch No. 2483: Conditions in Japan in October 1943

subfiles.about: Instructs the Chungking mission to continue transmitting Foreign Economic Administration intelligence reports on Japanese conditions as the Department does not receive them directly.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Hull instructs Chungking that State does not receive FEA reports directly and the mission should continue sending them.
subfiles.title: State Department Instruction No. 657 to Chungking: Receipt of FEA Reports
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Chungking

subfiles.about: Provides strategic suggestions to the OSS on psychological warfare and exploiting Japanese internal divisions and vulnerabilities to accelerate military defeat.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Grew advises OSS Director Donovan on morale operations: exploit Japanese social rigidity through rumors, simulated pamphlets and underground operations to widen military-public and Army-Navy rifts.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to Brigadier General William J. Donovan on Morale Operations against Japan
subfiles.to: Brigadier General William J. Donovan, Director, Office of Strategic Services

subfiles.about: Acknowledges and expresses gratitude for Ambassador Grew's recommendations regarding psychological and morale operations against Japan.
subfiles.from: William J. Donovan, Director, Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.summary: Donovan thanks Grew for his advice on morale operations against Japan, finding it penetrating and workable.
subfiles.title: Letter from William J. Donovan to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew: Acknowledging Advice on Morale Operations
subfiles.to: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, Department of State

subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese propaganda claims concerning the return of twenty-four commercial enterprises to the puppet Philippine government as an empty gesture.
subfiles.from: Paul P. Steintorf, Division of Philippine Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Steintorf shows the Japanese Army's return of 24 enterprises to the puppet Philippine Republic was empty propaganda, since seventeen were 'loaned back' to Japanese military management.
subfiles.title: Division of Philippine Affairs Memorandum: Japanese Army Returns Businesses to Puppet Philippine Republic

subfiles.about: Monitors enemy broadcasts covering the purported return of businesses to the Philippine Republic, religious affairs, and speeches by Laurel and Osias.
subfiles.from: Department of Information and Public Relations, Commonwealth of the Philippines
subfiles.summary: Enemy Radio Digest: Japanese transfer and leaseback of 24 Philippine enterprises, Japanese nuns returning from Manila, Laurel's address to women and Osias's university speech.
subfiles.title: Enemy Radio Digest, Vol. III, No. 22: Japanese Economic and Political Moves in the Philippines
subfiles.to: United States Government / Department of State

subfiles.about: Requests an urgent telegraphic summary of the State Department's interpretation of recent political and military developments in Japan.
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, American Consul, Colombo
subfiles.summary: Consul Bishop in Colombo requests an urgent summary of the Department's analysis of Japan's political crisis for SEAC liaison.
subfiles.title: Colombo Telegram No. 224: Request for Assessment of Japanese Political Changes

subfiles.about: Transmits the text of Joseph C. Grew's official statement analyzing the resignation of the Tojo Cabinet and cautioning against wishful thinking.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Hull sends Grew's July 20 statement: the Tojo cabinet's resignation proves military defeats and attempts to shore up morale, but Japan will still fight fanatically and the military remains in power.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to Colombo: Statement by Joseph C. Grew on the Resignation of the Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Transmits an article by former British Ambassador Sir Robert Craigie analyzing the fall of the Tojo Cabinet and the composition of the Koiso government.
subfiles.from: Dorsey Gassaway Fisher, Second Secretary of Embassy, London
subfiles.summary: Dorsey Fisher sends Craigie's July 31, 1944 Times article on the Saipan-driven crisis and the Koiso-Yonai team: coalition seeks broader support, but defeats will hasten militarism's collapse.
subfiles.title: London Despatch No. 17240: Times Article by Sir Robert Craigie on Political Changes in Japan

subfiles.about: Circulates excerpts from a 1942 Postal Censorship study detailing Japan's Greater East Asia policy and the totalitarian restructuring of the Diet under IRAPS.
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Max W. Bishop circulates excerpts from a June 1942 Hawaiian Postal Censorship report analyzing the ideological, territorial, and political foundations of Japan's Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. The report describes the vast geographic boundaries claimed by Japanese broadcasts and explains how the Tojo government centralized national power following the April 1942 Diet elections. It outlines the role of General Nobuyuki Abe and the establishment of the Imperial Rule Assistance Political Society (IRAPS / Taisei Yokusan Seijikai), which subordinated the Diet and corporate leadership under military-bureaucratic control within the constitutional framework.
subfiles.title: Office of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum and Report Excerpts: An Analysis of the GEA Policy and Its Political Background
subfiles.to: Files / FE Officers, Department of State

subfiles.about: Discusses script proposals for a joint State-CIAA radio series directed at Latin America depicting life under Japanese military occupation.
subfiles.from: John B. Carlile, Department of State / Allan H. Fry, Content Division, CIAA
subfiles.summary: Carlile records consultations with CIAA's Fry on radio programs on Japanese occupation for Latin America; State wants arguments grounded in Japanese customs, not melodrama.
subfiles.title: State Department and CIAA Memoranda: Proposed Radio Program Series on Japanese Occupation
subfiles.to: Allan H. Fry, CIAA / John B. Carlile, Department of State

subfiles.about: Transmits observations on Japanese domestic hardship, war morale, and Allied POWs supplied by former Swiss Consul at Kobe Maurice Champoud.
subfiles.summary: Steinhardt relays ex-Swiss Consul Champoud: Tokyo demolitions and evacuations, food shortages, public ignorance of casualties, rumors of Tojo's suicide, and his Formosa POW camp report.
subfiles.title: Ankara Telegram No. 1610 and Paraphrase: Report on Conditions in Japan by Former Swiss Consul Maurice Champoud

subfiles.about: Contains internal Division of Cultural Relations routing slips and referral notes regarding a file on the late Marquis Shigenobu Okuma.
subfiles.summary: These internal State Department routing slips and handwritten notes from the Division of Cultural Relations (CU), dated February 24-25, 1944, refer file material concerning Count (late Marquis) Shigenobu Okuma to Joseph W. Ballantine, Chief of the Division of Japanese Affairs (JA), for departmental consideration.
subfiles.title: Division of Cultural Relations Routing Slips: Reference Concerning Count Shigenobu Okuma
subfiles.to: Joseph W. Ballantine, Chief of the Division of Japanese Affairs

subfiles.about: Cross-references a State Department memorandum concerning Premier Koiso's address to the 85th Diet session, filed under 740.0011 P.W./9-744.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet (recorded in duplicate) referencing a September 7, 1944 memorandum by Kullgren concerning Premier Kuniaki Koiso's speech delivered to the 85th extraordinary session of the Japanese Diet. The reference indicates that the original paper is filed under decimal classification 740.0011 P.W./9-744.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Premier Koiso's Speech to the 85th Diet Session

subfiles.about: Transmits translations of three articles from the Yenan newspaper Giefang Rhbao describing rural hardships, factory sabotage, and urban food shortages in Japan.
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Ambassador, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss transmits English translations prepared by the Co-ordinated Translation Center in Chungking of three articles from the March 27, 1944 issue of the Yenan Chinese Communist newspaper Giefang Rhbao. The first article details extreme physical strain, excessive working hours, and severe food deficits experienced by women farm laborers in Inokuchi village, Saitama Prefecture. The second translation describes widespread slowdowns, absenteeism, and strikes in Japanese munitions factories, dockyards, and Kyushu mines despite draconian military supervision. The third describes severe rice shortages in Tokyo and the weekly phenomenon of 'purchasing troops'—trainloads of urban residents traveling to rural areas like Chiba to procure black-market produce.
subfiles.title: Chungking Despatch No. 3013: Translations of Articles on Japanese Conditions from Yenan Communist Newspaper Giefang Rhbao

subfiles.about: Transmits a report by John S. Service from Yenan containing an interview with Susumu Okano outlining the postwar revolutionary program of the Japanese Communist Party.
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Ambassador, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Gauss forwards John Service's interview with Susumu Okano (Nosaka): a three-stage program from ending war to democracy to socialism, resembling Chinese Communist doctrine.
subfiles.title: Chungking Despatch No. 3021: Program of the Japanese Communist Party
